sources.citation: de Vries, Lourens. 2004. A short grammar of Inanwatan: an endangered language of the Bird's Head of Papua, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics 560. Canberra: ANU. Appendix 3 intro p.129; sec. 5 'Benawa word list' pp.153-154; acknowledgements p.viii.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: SILENT for Kaburi. p.153: 'the Benawa (or Kaburi) language is spoken by about 1000 people. The following list was taken (in the Indonesian spelling) by the anthropologist Dianne van Oosterhout in the village Sumano, in April 1997'. 93-item list, no stress marks, no phonological prose. (Inanwatan proper has 'unpredictable, lexical word stress', p.25 -- a different language.)

sources.citation: Berry, Keith & Christine Berry. 1987. A survey of the South Bird's Head Stock. Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 4: 81-117. Abepura: Universitas Cenderawasih & SIL. (Kaburi: sec. 3.1 p.84; sec. 3.2.3 p.87; sec. 3.3 'Phonological features' p.89; sec. 4.3.3 'Kaburi' p.93; village table p.98; Appendix C comparative word lists pp.99-117.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: SILENT. Sec. 3.3 (p.89, for the whole stock): languages 'generally do not allow word final consonants and there are very few consonant clusters.. simple VCV or CVCV syllabic structure'; nothing on stress/accent. Sec. 4.3.3 (p.93): c.600 speakers, north of Kokoda, 'The data only comes from one informant who was interviewed in Kalitami.' Appendix C (p.99) states the apostrophe marks a glottal stop, so the Kaburi list (kohe'a, to'ah, wa'ava..) carries no stress marks.
